newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-VW unveils fourth generation of Golf.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-VW unveils fourth generation of Golf.

text.p: Volkswagen AG, unveiling the fourth generation of the world's best-selling Golf model, has set an ambitious goal of selling two million of the vehicles a year in the mid-term, sources at the German carmaker said on Tuesday.

VW expects explosive demand for the new model, which was shown to the media for the first time on Tuesday in Bonn, and believe it can meet customer demand without adding new plants or boosting its full-time workforce, the sources told Reuters.

In addition, VW officials say they will aggressively price the new Golf against chief European market competitors such as General Motor Corp's new Opel Astra model, due to go on sale next April, and the Escort from Ford Motor Co.

The new Golf, which usually commands a premium, is expected to be priced at about 25,000 marks ($13,600) compared with the current base price of 24,000 marks. The higher price is in part due to better standard equipment in the new Golf.

"The market analysis shows excellent demand for the new Golf," one VW source said. He declined to be more specific as to how long it will take VW to ramp up Golf production toward two million vehicles from the 1996 level of about 700,000.

VW chief executive Ferdinand Piech said in a television interview late on Monday that VW expects to sell at least 700,000 of the new Golf models in Europe alone in the first year after the car goes on sale in October.

"It is without a doubt the bread from which we live," said VW spokesman Klaus Kocks, noting that the Golf accounts for half of the Volkswagen brand's output and a fifth of all cars sold within the group that includes Audi, SEAT and Skoda.
VW investors are cheering the new model, seen as one reason for VW shares more than doubling in price so far this year.

"Should sales be successful, then we expect clearly more gains in VW shares," said ABN Amro Bank in a report, noting VW shares could climb to 2,300 marks in the next 12 to 18 months from the current level of about 1,350 marks.
Volkswagen has put much effort into designing the new Golf, which originally made its debut in March 1974. It has been the backbone of VW's sales and nearly 18 million have now been produced.

While the new Golf shows a lot of family resemblance, the car has been revamped with bolder styling lines to make it longer and roomier than the current model as well as to make important improvements in safety, such as side air bags.
"It's what customers want," Piech said in the television interview, commenting on the likeness to old Golf models. But he quickly added, "It's a totally new car from top to bottom."

VW, the fourth-largest carmaker in the world, is counting on the Golf to help anchor is global sales as it seeks to improve profitability by cutting costs through a plan to reduce the number of platforms within the group to four from 16.

Critics have charged that VW risks cannibalising sales by producing too many cars on the same platforms, such as the hot-selling Audi A3 compact which has hurt Golf sales since it is built on the same platform and share many similarities.
But VW executives, including Piech, have said that the some 50 vehicles now offered within the VW group have their own distinct stylings to attract a broader range of customers.
The new Golf will face a tough market in the compact class, in part due to the launch by Mercedes-Benz of the A-class subcompact and new model offerings from Opel and Ford.

Another pressing issue for VW is the emergence of smaller minivans, such as the Renault Scenic which has helped the French carmaker reach a 12 percent market share in Europe at a time when leader VW remains stagnant at 21 percent.
Opel will also offer the Zafira in late 1998, a small minivan based on the Astra platform that can carry up to seven people and will be priced aggressively against the Golf.
"I think VW will have to go beyond their normal market for the Golf and try to extend the reach with the new one," said Jonathan Storey at European Automotive Research in Britain.
"The new Golf is conservatively styled and that may be a problem. There are signs that the European market is ready for bolder designs," Storey said. "Just look at Renault's success."

($ = 1.834 German Marks)
